prompt.context: It is 2009. Wally's Wire Factory makes electronics cables. Like most players in the industry, Wally's Wire Factory makes a large range of cables, wires, connectors, converters, and basic electronics extras. It has a steady stream of business and has little desire to expand into new products. Wally's Wire Factory has hired you to help increase profitability from its existing businesses.
prompt.question: How can Wally's Wire Factory increase profitability from its existing businesses?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors and how competitive is the market?
clarifying_info.a: There are significant barriers to entry; no new competitors in the past 5 years; Wally's projects it would take 2-3 years for a new competitor to enter. Competition varies significantly by region.
Wally's is the leader of an established mature industry that is growing at the rate of GDP. Provide Exhibit #1 and Exhibit #2 (market share data).

clarifying_info.q: What kinds of products does Wally's sell?
clarifying_info.a: There is a range of higher and lower end products, and margins vary considerably by product line.
Customers are mainly IT departments and retail businesses, but there is a sizable number of technology-minded individuals who make direct purchases as well.

exhibits.title: Wire Market Share Data, 2006
exhibits.shows: Pie or bar chart of wire market share by competitor across regions in 2006
exhibits.data: Market share breakdown for Wally's Wire Factory, Competitor 1, Competitor 2, Competitor 3 across North America, Europe, and Asia for year 2006

exhibits.title: Wire Market Share Data, 2009
exhibits.shows: Pie or bar chart of wire market share by competitor across regions in 2009, enabling comparison to 2006
exhibits.data: Market share breakdown for Wally's Wire Factory, Competitor 1, Competitor 2, Competitor 3 across North America, Europe, and Asia for year 2009

framework: Segment the analysis by geography (North America, Europe, Asia) to identify where profitability improvement is feasible
Assess competitive dynamics and pricing power in each region using market share trends (Exhibits 1 & 2)
Focus on North America where Wally's has the strongest position and faces less commoditization pressure
Analyze product-level margin variation to identify sources of profitability improvement
Examine the relationship between price elasticity and gross margin by product to identify pricing opportunities
Develop targeted pricing recommendations: raise prices on inelastic products with low margins; selectively cut prices on elastic products with high margins to gain share

questions.prompt: What happened over the past three years (2006 to 2009)? Reference Exhibits 1 and 2.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare the two market share charts region by region and draw strategic implications. Key observations: (1) Wally's North America share has grown — weak buyer power since the product is a small component of buyer costs. (2) Competitor 1 has grown considerably in Europe mainly at Wally's expense — likely through price reductions, threatening Wally's margins there. (3) Competition in Asia has become fierce; Competitor 1 grew at expense of Competitor 3; all firms splitting profits suggests late-stage pricing parity. Candidate should note that market share data alone cannot indicate absolute market growth.

questions.prompt: In which market are we best able to increase profitability from existing businesses, and how should we approach this?
questions.guidance: Europe and Asia are unlikely candidates because the product is being commoditized in those regions. North America is the best opportunity given Wally's strong and growing position there and the absence of extreme competition. Since margins vary by product line, the next step is to understand the causes of those variations within North America.

questions.prompt: We want to understand variations in margins across products in North America. We will plot gross margin by product on the y-axis. What variable(s) might we want to plot on the x-axis? (Exhibit 3 shown — candidate suggests axis)
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies price elasticity as the key x-axis variable, since there may be room to capture value through pricing in North America. The candidate should also explain at least one data pattern that would come with a strategic recommendation. Other reasonable variables (e.g., volume, product age, cost structure) may be accepted but the price elasticity angle is strongest given the strategic context.

questions.prompt: If we choose to chart price elasticity on the x-axis, what kind of pattern might we expect in the scatter plot?
questions.guidance: Products with high price elasticity typically have the lowest gross margins because they are close substitutes and consumers shop on price. Products with low price elasticity have relatively high gross margins because they don't substitute well and consumers choose on features. Therefore the expected pattern is a clear downward trend: as price elasticity increases, gross margin decreases. Any pattern that does NOT show a clear downward trend would indicate room to improve profitability through price adjustments.

questions.prompt: After plotting price elasticity vs. gross margin by product, we produce the chart shown. There appears to be little correlation between price elasticity and gross margin. What do you conclude? (Exhibit 5)
questions.guidance: The lack of correlation means pricing is misaligned with demand sensitivity. Candidate should identify three actionable zones: (1) Lower-left quadrant (low elasticity, low margin): raise prices — we can substantially increase margin without suffering share losses since demand is inelastic. (2) Upper-right quadrant (high elasticity, high margin): cut prices — we can substantially increase share with only slight margin loss since demand is elastic. (3) Revenue increases upper-left through price, and upper-right through volume.

brainstorming.prompt: What variable(s) might we want to plot on the x-axis when examining gross margin variation by product?

recommendation: Focus profitability improvement efforts on North America, where Wally's has a strong and growing market position and faces less commoditization pressure than in Europe or Asia
In Europe and Asia, avoid aggressive pricing moves as the product is commoditizing; monitor and defend share without sacrificing margin further

Within North America, pursue a dual pricing strategy: raise prices on products with low price elasticity and currently low gross margins (lower-left quadrant), and lower prices on products with high price elasticity and currently high gross margins (upper-right quadrant) to drive volume growth
risks: Competitors in North America could react to price increases with aggressive counter-pricing, eroding Wally's share
Price cuts in high-elasticity segments may trigger a race to the bottom if competitors follow
Misclassification of products into elasticity quadrants due to data limitations could lead to suboptimal pricing decisions
next_steps: Conduct detailed product-level analysis to confirm price elasticity estimates and validate the scatter plot findings
Model the revenue and margin impact of proposed price changes before implementation
Explore cost reduction opportunities across product lines to complement the pricing strategy
Monitor European and Asian markets for further deterioration and set triggers for strategic reassessment
